utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Registrar, please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Today is Tuesday, 18th of November, 2008. Good afternoon to the accused, to the Defence counsel, the representatives of the OTP, and all the people assisting us. Very well. I note that Mr. Praljak is absent. He must be ill. There's a virus going around. I, myself, do my best to be present. Mr. Registrar, I think you have two IC numbers for us.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honours. The first one is in regards to the Prlic Defence objection to Prosecution exhibits tendered through Witness Batinic, that will be assigned IC 00886. The next one, Your Honours, is Prosecution response to exhibits tendered by Prlic Defence through Witness Batinic, which will be assigned IC 00887. And the third one, which is request for admission of exhibits tendered through the Witness Batinic will be Exhibit IC 00888, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Mr. Scott, you may proceed. Oh, but we need a witness for you to continue. Yes, Mr. Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: While we're waiting for witness, the Praljak Defence also submitted IC list, and it was on time to the Registrar, but it was not read today. Perhaps it is because Mr. Chuka is not here. We can do that later, just be on the safe side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, our legal officer is going to check with the Registrar or the court deputy. Of course, you'll have an IC number for your list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, we are going to continue with the cross-examination. I don't know whether Mr. Scott will finish today or whether your testimony finishes today. If Mr. Karnavas can't finish his redirect, we will continue tomorrow. Mr. Scott, yes. Witness, do you have anything to say or are you not available at all tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not available tomorrow, because my wife is travelling and I have to take charge of our children. They're very small, three years old and one and a half years old respectively, so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I'm asking everybody to do their best so that you can mind your children tomorrow. Mr. Scott, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good afternoon, Your Honours, to each of you, and to all those in and around the courtroom, and also Mr. Tomic, good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. Tomic, just to finish off on some topics that we got to -- reached a bit at the end of the day yesterday, I'd like to start by showing you Exhibit P10657. It will be in the third binder, 10657, and I'll be most appreciative, sir, if we can move as efficiently as possible. You've just heard that we'd like to accommodate you as much as we can, if we can, and if we can move efficiently, that will be in everyone's interests, sir. P10657. Just some very basic points on this document, sir. I think you'll find it rather straightforward. This is a set of decisions issued over the name of Ivan Bender, as acting prime minister. On the first page, the first decision in the bundle, if you will, appears to be a decision dismissing Mr. Jadranko Prlic as prime minister of the government of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna, signed on the 15th of June, 1996; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And would that generally be consistent with whatever memory you might still have of that situation? If not the exact day, sir, but sometime in approximately mid-1996, Mr. Prlic ceased acting as prime minister of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If you go to the second decision, please, Roman numeral II on the same document, essentially, in Roman numeral II I think you'll find -- can you confirm, please, that pursuant to that order, Mr. Valentin Coric and Mr. Pero Markovic, among others, are dismissed as vice-prime ministers of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna, and likewise, sir, please, if you go to Roman numeral III, it says: "Dismissed as members of the Government of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna are the following:" And for present purposes, I'll simply mention number 4, Neven Tomic, and number 5, Mr. Kozulj. Actually, we can pass -- actually, we can go over to the next page. You also see Bozo Rajic, for example, Jozo Maric, and the Vladislav Pogarcic that has come up several times in your testimony. Can you likewise confirm, sir, in general that it was around the middle of 1996 that you and these others were, if you will, left your positions in the government of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Thank you for that. I'd like you to next turn, please, sir, to Exhibit P10704. It will again be in the third binder, P10704. Now, in coming to this exhibit, sir, you'll remember yesterday that I suggested to you or I asked you, in any event, whether it was not the case that by the fall of 1993, there began to be discussions moving away from any notion that each of the three ethnic groups, Croat, Serb, Muslim, would have their own separate unit or entity, whichever word one wants to use, and there was moving -- there was some movement in the direction of what became -- it may not have been the exact terminology at the time, but what became ultimately the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina. You remember those questions; correct?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, was it around that time, sir, that in addition to talking about federation, there began to be discussion about something called a confederation that would exist comprising the federation, that is, the joint Muslim-Croat Federation as one unit, if you will, of the confederation, and the Republic of Croatia as the second unit, if you will, of the confederation.

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was part of the Washington Agreement. It was the pre-confederal agreement between Croatia and the federation.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And, sir, was it around that time, do you recall that I think there was a saying, if I remember correctly, there was a saying that was going around at least in some of the circles, some of the political circles at that time, to the effect of "No federation without confederation"? Do you remember anything like that?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there was insistence on the implementation of the Washington Agreement as a whole. The Bosnian side refused to discuss the pre-confederal contract. They only wanted to talk about the latter part of the Washington Agreement, which was about access to the port of Ploce through Neum, and then the --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I'm trying to do this for both our benefits, sir, because of the time issue. My specific question was not about access to the sea, but did there become -- was this saying -- did this saying evolve, and I think you've answered the question, "Yes." So my next question following on that was: Do you recall where that saying originated? Who coined the phrase, if you remember?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, this normally came from Mr. Bender.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If you can look, please, to Exhibit P10704, the one that I asked you to turn to a moment ago, and indeed this is an interview, in large part, of -- excuse me, interview with Mr. Bender in a BBC article dated the 15th of June, 1994, with the source being Croatian Radio in Zagreb at 1500 Greenwich Mean Time on the 13th of June, 1994; and I'd like to direct your attention, please, to about halfway down the page, after you get through some of the introductory material, in brackets, I think you will see the first bracket of Mr. Bender's name, and if I can direct you to find that, please, just by way of orientation. In that paragraph, Mr. Bender says: "In the beginning, it ought to be stressed that this meeting was organised while the delegation of the Croat Republic of Herceg-Bosna was paying a visit to Zagreb on the occasion of Croatia's statehood day. Mr. Jadranko Prlic and Mr. Pero Markovic led the delegation." Skipping one paragraph, sir, in the next paragraph it goes on to say -- Mr. Bender goes on to say: "We should stress again that the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina and its organisation is closely connected with the establishment of the confederation with Croatia. This is a package, because without the establishment of the confederation, there can be no federation. This should be clear to all of us, and it should be repeated that this is a package that is, in practice, a sort of unity about which there should be no discussion on this occasion." And would you consider, sir, that Mr. Bender here is accurately stating the position of the HVO and Herceg-Bosna leadership at that time in June 1994?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was not a generally valid position. He was more sort of under the influence of the fact that he was president of the Neum HVO, itself a town that was discussed in the latter part of the Washington Agreement. Whenever speaking in public, he was adamant that this should be the approach. Essentially, nevertheless, this was about the implementation of the Washington Agreement as a package that was signed as such.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If I can ask you to go on to the next paragraph, please. The second line of that paragraph goes on to say: "The bodies of the Croat Republic of Herceg-Bosna and Herceg-Bosna itself are going to exist until the package which I have mentioned has been established. There can be no talk about the suspension of the government of the Croat Republic of Herceg-Bosna. On the contrary, it should further be strengthened until the federation and the confederation have been established." And again my question to you, sir: Not in every detail, perhaps not in every nuance, but was that the position of the HVO and Herceg-Bosna leadership at this time?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The position of the leadership was to see the Washington Agreement implemented as signed, which included the establishment of the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the drafting of other documents that were part of the Washington Agreement; access to the port of Ploce, free passage through Neum, as well as a pre-confederal agreement that was itself part and parcel of the Washington Agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Please answer my specific question further on this. It was the position of the HVO and the Herceg-Bosna authorities at this time that Herceg-Bosna as an entity, as described here, the government of the Croat Republic of Herceg-Bosna, it would continue, there would be no discussion of its ending. It would continue until the federation and the confederation with Croatia had been established. That was the HVO Herceg-Bosna position; correct?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what the Washington Agreement states. The existing administration arrangement, that being Herceg-Bosna --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... on this. My question to you is very clear. You keep saying it was the Washington -- you're saying that was the Washington Agreement position, but that was not the position of the HVO? You didn't share that position? The Herceg-Bosna and HVO leadership had a different position?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, but in this case the position was the same, as I pointed out before. Before the establishment of the Federation and the federal institutions, there was the existing administrative arrangement in place and it was operating. Pensions were paid, schools were paid for, until the federal institutions were established, and that is precisely what I was saying before. Therefore, there was this transitional period throughout which Herceg-Bosna continued to operate pursuant to the transitional provisions enshrined in the Washington Agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If you'll go next, please, to P10696, P10696 also in the same binder. Sir, this is another BBC article about six months later, 12 December 1994, reporting coverage again on Croatian Radio Zagreb in Croatia on the 10th of December, actually broadcast apparently on the 10th of December, 1994. It talks about a meeting and the issuance of a statement from the president, from President Tudjman's office. It appears that among other people, you were present on this day, reading down the first longer paragraph. Mr. Zubak and Mr. Prlic, Neven Tomic and a number of other people. For present purposes, sir, if I can just direct your attention to the next-to-last paragraph: "President Tudjman said that Croatia strongly supported the creation of the Federation and its confederation with Croatia and that the Croat Republic of Herceg-Bosna would remain in existence until the federation and the confederation started functioning." Now, you were at this meeting, apparently, and do you agree that that was the gist or position that President Tudjman and the Herceg-Bosna delegation -- that was their position at, again, this time in December 1994?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. That's perfectly in keeping with what I said, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, in --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, sorry for interrupting. I'll be very brief, because this is a very relevant topic and no error is allowed. If I understand you properly, the Washington Agreement, from what you yourself have said, basically recognised the existence of the Republic of Herceg-Bosna, but as said by President Tudjman by the documents admitted to you by the Prosecutor, the Republic of Herceg-Bosna is supposed to continue to function until the federation or the confederation with Croatia is created, is established. Until they start operating, the Republic of Herceg-Bosna is supposed to be operational and exist. Is that what you said? And you say this is further to the spirit of the Washington Agreement. Of course, we are going to have a close look at this, but since you were one of the players at the time, you might provide us with an answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Washington Agreement, as I said, envisaged the establishment of new federal institutions, starting with the federal government, the federal customs, the central bank, and so on and so forth. It does not provide for the abolishment of Herceg-Bosna or for the possibility of joining the existing republican institutions. Rather, it envisages the establishment of new ones. There are the transitional provisions saying that the existing administrative arrangements, which is how they referred to Herceg-Bosna, would remain in power until new federal institutions were established. The moment a new set of federal customs was established, the Herceg-Bosna customs would be abolished, but also the customs of Bosnia and Herzegovina. As soon as there was a tax administration for the federation, the one for Bosnia-Herzegovina and for the Republic of Herceg-Bosna would be abolished and would cease to operate. So that's what the resistance to the implementation of the Washington Agreement was about, because the Bosniak side was adamant that Herceg-Bosna should be abolished, no more than that, and that we should enjoin the existing institutions that already existed in the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. But that was not the substance of the Washington Agreement. This was eventually acknowledged prior to the Dayton Accords, when the agreement on the implementation of the federation was signed, and the federation government was separated from the republican government, and then federal institutions started to be established. As those were being established, the institutions of Herceg-Bosna were gradually dwindling; the payment bureau, the customs, the financial police, and I'm talking about all the institutions in the areas in which I, myself, was operating.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One final question. You said that there was an agreement to revitalise before the Dayton Agreement. This is page 11, line 6. But who signed this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This agreement was signed by Mr. Zubak and Mr. Ganic, if I'm not mistaken. They were the president and the vice-president of the Federation. In America, too, on the eve of the -- or rather maybe it was in Vienna. It was on the eve of the Dayton talks, when it became clear that the current state could -- was no longer viable and when it became clear that the Bosniak side had certain guarantees that the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina would continue to exist as the new Bosnia and Herzegovina under the Dayton Agreement. And at that time, they agreed for the government of the federation and the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina to become separate entities, and that's when the real process of establishing the federation actually began.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if you allow me, I would just like to point out that there is an error which is highly relevant, and it might lead to misunderstandings when you try to compare the testimony of the witness with the Washington Agreements. At page 10, line 18, the witness said that the term "regional arrangements," which was a term used for Herceg-Bosna in the Washington Agreements, and as far as I understood the witness, he was talking about the administrative arrangement, and it was in fact the term "administrative arrangement" that was used in the Washington Agreements. This was the designation for Herceg-Bosna in those agreements, so I think that this might be quite relevant, and could perhaps the witness be asked to explain?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you agree, Witness, that this administrative arrangement in the agreement had to do with the Republic of Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "The existing administrative arrangement," that is the language of the Washington Agreement, "the existing administrative arrangement."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, just to finish up on this topic, and again I would be most appreciative if you can be brief on this, and in fact it fits in with what you were just saying a moment ago: During the interim period between Washington, which was signed in February, parts in March, 1994, and the Dayton Peace agreement in November, 1995, is it correct, sir, that during that period the federation never became a functioning structure? The federation did not essentially come into existence any time prior to Dayton; correct?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The institutions were not established, as I've already explained, so that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And the confederation between the federation and the Republic of Croatia, that was never established at any time; correct?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, do you agree that in this horrible conflict that all of us are here -- the reason for all of us being here in this room, in fact, that during this horrible conflict all sides created crimes -- committed crimes, and there were victims on all sides? Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And can you tell us -- can you tell the Judges, please, and following up on that, what were some of the crimes committed by the HVO?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I'm not wrong, this is the factual -- the witness on facts. How he can know whether the crimes were committed and who committed what? The question before that was maybe of general nature, but this one is, I think, too far. Maybe for the expert. But on the end this is the issue on which the Trial Chamber should respond.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, not at all, not at all. This man, he says crimes were committed by the HVO. He was a senior official throughout this time period. He's obviously an educated, intelligent man, and he must have had some views. He didn't have this in a vacuum, unless he had his head in the sand the entire time and he must had some ideas when he says, "Yes, I agree, crimes were committed on all sides." And I think the Chamber should hear and we should hear what his views are on that. It's not beyond his capabilities at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Scott, it strikes me that's an extremely vague, broad, open question. I don't see what advantage the Chamber could draw from an answer. If the witness says, "I know there were rapes committed, there were murders, there were killings, there was arson," what use should this be to the --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Perhaps the better word would be "incidents."

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You're saying that throughout this conflict, places like Achmici, Stupni Do, Stolac, Heliodrom, the Mostar siege, that this man didn't know about any of those things? Is that what the Chamber is suggesting?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: It sounds a bit like fishing, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, it's not at all, Your Honour. I want to probe this man's position and credibility, and I think it's directly relevant and I couldn't disagree more with Your Honour Judge Trechsel on this point. This man can be asked questions to state his views on this, and it goes to his credit, among other things. He was sitting in Mostar a few metres away from where crimes were being committed on a daily basis --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Scott. -- and you're saying it's not relevant, what he knows?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, you had another possibility, a forensic possibility, to deal with the subject, because you presented a presidential transcript mentioning Stupni Do, and you did not put any questions on Stupni Do. You put questions on something else. I, myself, indicated that the meeting was held following the Stupni Do events, so based on that you could have asked him whether he learned of events in Ahmici, Stupni Do. He could have said "yes" or "no." In the affirmative, you could have put follow-up question. If he had said "no," that was it, and this way we would not have had a flurry of lawyers on their feet, such as a wave raging over the courtroom, in order to raise objections.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, Counsel. It wasn't a wave over the courtroom. One counsel got on their feet, and so it's a bit of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I saw two of them. I saw Mr. Karnavas as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, the point of this is -- excuse me. The point of this is, to respond to the Judge's question, the point of this is, Your Honour, yes, I could have proceeded that way and I could go through a series of questions, "How about Stupni Do, how about the Heliodrom, how about Stolac," how about this, how about that? Yes, I could proceed that way. There's absolutely nothing wrong with asking the witness to tell us, what does he remember, what struck him at that time, what does he tell us? When he says he agrees that crimes were committed on his side, so to speak, why can't he tell us that? I'm at a complete loss as to why the Chamber or anyone in the courtroom finds that objectionable. It's a question that the witness can answer and directly relevant, among other things, to his credit.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Mr. President, unless -- first of all, he can lay a foundation that he was in Stupni Do, that he was in Ahmici and what have you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: He doesn't have to be there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Excuse me, let me speak. I suggest that you keep quiet for a second. Now, unless he can establish a foundation, this question is out of order. That's number 1. Number 2 and more importantly, the Court has already ruled. I suggest that they now -- that you now instruct Mr. Scott to move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: The Court has not ruled. The Court has tended to give some guidance, if you will, and with the greatest respect to the Chamber, I don't think there's anything improper about the way I have proceeded with it and so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't want to add too much to the flurry or whatever. I'm curious what the word was in French, if that's the collective noun for lawyers, Your Honour, but we do wish to support what Mr. Kovacic said and to draw this distinction: Now, Mr. Scott asked a very general question which was inviting the witness to agree that, broadly speaking, these things happened on all sides. But to move from that to crimes, there's a legal element to crimes. The point that is included in what my learned friends have been saying is if Mr. Scott had wanted, in the way that Your Honour Judge Antonetti suggested it, Mr. Scott had wanted to ask the witness specifically in relation to events about which he has knowledge, that's another matter, but when you move to crimes, there's a legal element to that and, Your Honour, that is, as Mr. Kovacic made clear, that's a matter for the Trial Chamber and the question isn't appropriate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Judges are going to deliberate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: No translation.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The mike was on, but there seems to be a technical problem again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It seems to be working now from this console. Very well. It should be okay now. I was saying that after deliberating, the Trial Chamber is of the view that you can ask questions, but they have to be related to events, to incidents. You can ask the witness about whether he was aware or he heard of Stupni Do. But regarding the legal ingredients of crimes, that's a much more difficult issue, and the Trial Chamber considers that you are not to tackle the questions from that point of view.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, let's come at it this way.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If you can turn to, sir, Exhibit P10715, which will be again in the third binder of documents, P10715. This is a report by the BBC dated the 20th of August, 1993, based on a report coming on Croatian Radio Herceg-Bosna, Mostar, on the 18th of August, 1993. This covers an apparent letter from Mr. Prlic to Lord Owen and Mr. Stoltenberg, and about two-thirds of the way down, a little over halfway down through the text of the document, it says: "Dear Sirs. We used these tragic examples to draw your attention to the continued inhuman conduct on the part of the members of the Muslim armed forces in The War against local Croats. We have every reason to believe that the perpetrated crimes," apparently Mr. Prlic didn't have any problem using the word "crime," " ... perpetrated crimes, genocide and ethnic cleansing are in accordance with the overall goals of the Muslim struggle, although these acts are in blatant contravention of international humanitarian law and all Geneva Conventions on the conduct of war," apparently known by Mr. Prlic. "We believe that by ignoring such conduct, or by describing it as excesses and actions carried out by certain individuals or independent groups, the international bodies and media create great hatred towards and lack of trust in the people performing peace-making or humanitarian actions on the part of the entire Croatian nation ..." Now, isn't the point that Mr. Prlic is making here, at least attempting to make to the people he's addressed this to is that these crimes should not be dismissed as individual bad acts, but in Mr. Prlic's view, these crimes were being driven, if you will, from the top down; they were coordinated, they were organised, they were based on policy, correct, according to Mr. Prlic? Sir, please.

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what it says.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you answer my question?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what it says in the letter.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Doesn't -- isn't that the point here, and using Mr. Prlic's own words, is -- I mean, isn't what happened, sir, and isn't what you've heard -- you've certainly heard said, in the last 10 or 15 years, that it seems to be when the crimes are committed, if we can use the terminology, by the other side, they were organised, they were driven by policy, et cetera, as Mr. Prlic says here, but when crimes were committed, if you will, if you'll allow me to say, by your side or by the ethnic group that you most closely identify with, then the explanation is always, "Well, they were individual bad acts, but nothing more than that"; haven't you heard that, sir, being said by all three groups, Muslims, Serbs, Croats, during and since the war ended?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this was the usual language.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Do you agree with Mr. Prlic, that to characterize crimes in that way and just say, "Well, these are just individual bad acts," is often a mischaracterisation and, in fact, a minimisation of such conduct?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I personally think that they should be seen in the framework of other activities that were going on in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Well, let's turn to -- let's turn to Exhibit 1D 01883, which will be in the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: There's no translation, Your Honour. My apologies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will -- can you hear, please? I repeat. Witness, Witness, I'm wondering whether Mr. Scott did not make a broad interpretation of this text, in looking at the transcript of the letter that Mr. Prlic sent to Lord Owen and Mr. Stoltenberg, where he recalls that there were crimes. But in this letter, he refers to individuals, independent groups, but do you read the fact that in addition to individuals and independent groups, there's a complete -- a whole organisation? I don't believe that's written, and yet Mr. Scott seems to be saying that. What do you think of that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is, first of all, a reaction to the assessments by the international bodies and the media to the attacks, murders, destruction of property of Croats, and to the interpretation thereof as individual, isolated cases. And that is why, in this letter, Mr. Prlic says that if these cases continue to be treated as individual, isolated cases, that among the Croat people this engenders a feeling that the international bodies are not fair, that they do not treat all the parties in Bosnia and Herzegovina in the same equitable manner. And he stresses that this is part of an organised drive, organised activities, on the part of the Bosniak side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very good.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, sir, that's exactly my point, and perhaps the courtroom might understand the concept of moving from the more specific to the general, and this point could be made about -- sir, I put to you that this one may be about something that happened in this particular instance that's reported here. But could -- I put to you the same thing could be said about Ahmici, the same thing could be said about Stupni Do, the same thing could be said about Muslims being forced out of Capljina and Stolac. And if one of the Muslim leaders was writing this letter instead of Mr. Prlic, presumably they would be saying the same thing. And my point to you, sir, and the point that I was trying to pursue with the Chamber, not misrepresenting this particular document, was: Isn't that -- wasn't that common to what all sides did? And if it's on your side, it's an individual bad act; if it's the other side, they're all organised, all policy driven, et cetera? That's what you've experienced in the dialogue during and after the war, isn't it? And previously you said, if I can remind you, some minutes ago before all the interventions, you said, "Yes." Correct?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, if we can turn to a document which I hoped to get to about 15 minutes ago, 1D 01183 in the third -- excuse me, in the fourth binder, in the smaller of the binders. If we can have the assistance -- thank you, sir. We're going back to a report of an HVO HZ-HB meeting on the 18th of March, 1993, and I would like to turn your attention, please, on -- under what's the agenda item 4, not in the list of agenda items but as we get into the text of the document. You'll see a series of headings "AD 1," "AD 2," "AD 3," "AD 4." If you go to "AD 4," if you can find that, please, I believe it will be on the second page of the Croatian version, second page of the English version. Under that heading there is a paragraph that says: "Mr. S. Bozic," I take that to be Slobodan Bozic, the deputy minister of -- or deputy head of the Department of Defence: "Mr. S. Bozic stated that in accordance with the previous conclusion of the HZ-HB HVO, drafts of the above-listed decrees have been composed, but an opinion on them must be sought from the Finance Department of the HZ-HB HVO." Now, sir, this is taking us some ways back in the course of your testimony, since you first came some weeks ago, but does this not remind us and confirm again that one of the functions of your department, the Finance Department, was to review proposed HVO decisions and decrees to determine, if you will, their financial impact, how they would be financially provided for if, in fact, such policies or decisions went forward and were carried out? Correct?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but only to establish whether they were financially viable and whether funds were earmarked for them in the budget.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now if we'll next please go to P05610 in binder number 2. P05610. Sir, this is a record of another HVO HZ-HB meeting on the 4th of October, 1993, and I would like to turn your particular attention to the bottom of -- item 1, which is on the bottom of the first page in the English version, and I believe likewise the bottom of the first page of the Croatian version. Mr. Stojic intervenes and says: "Mr. Bruno Stojic raised an objection in relation to item 7 of the draft minutes, claiming that he did not attend the previous meeting. He argued that the conclusion dealing with the method of claiming expenses for fuel used to evacuate expelled persons from Kakanj should be amended, considering that the cost of fuel should be borne by the Office for Displaced Persons and Refugees, and not the Department of Defence. The proposed amendment to the conclusion was adopted unanimously ..." Sir, does this reflect in not only this particular instance but discussions and decisions by the HVO from time to time over who should bear -- what department, what agency, should bear certain costs?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. This was a situation in which fuel, this company Interina provided the fuel, and we did the monthly calculation for all the departments in the HVO. The accounts were settled, the taxes were collected, and the fuel was paid once every month. And then it was charged to a particular department, and the intention here was to say that the overall quality of fuel in this report was stated as if the Department of Defence consumed all of it, and this increased their expenditures, whereas in the actual fact, some of the fuel was used to evacuate the refugees. And when Mr. Stojic raised the objection, then this was charged to the Office for Refugees, where it should have actually been charged.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, keeping these last two documents in mind, and also being mindful of your previous testimony on these topics, did the HVO government ever discuss where the funding and where the cost should be borne, the cost of arresting and detaining thousands of Muslim men in the summer of 1993?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already said in my testimony that the budget was passed for the first time in 1994, and up until that time no funds were earmarked.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'm not asking about the budget. I'm saying you've said -- we've just seen now, we saw it ten days ago, two weeks ago, other instances where the decisions would come to you, your Finance Department would have to say, "We have to provide for this, how are we going to fund it, what's going to happen, what are the financial costs of this policy or decision?" There was a decision in the summer of 1993 to arrest and detain a large number of -- thousands of Muslim men. Now, who was going to pay for the cost of that? How were those funds financed, how was that to be provided? It has nothing to do with whether there was a budget or not, sir. What decisions did the HVO HZ-HB take to provide for those financial needs?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The decisions were made on the basis of requests, requests -- and there were no requests for this kind of expenditure.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: So where did those funds, to your knowledge, come from, sir, the funds to -- whatever was spent to arrest these men, to put them in various places, to provide them food or not, to provide them medical services or not, where did these funds come from, then?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, underlying this budgetary aspect on the allocation of funds for fuel, there's a more important problem. Mr. Stojic intervenes. You are present at this meeting. Mr. Stojic intervenes to discuss the evacuees from Kakanj. To my knowledge, the evacuees of Kakanj are the Croats who are leaving Kakanj. Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good. So the Croats who are leaving Kakanj are expelled not by the Croats but by the Muslims, who apparently are launching an offensive, and there the transport cost for the Croats must be charged to the budget of the office and not the Department of Defence. This is what Mr. Stojic seems to be saying. You may not have a recollection of that meeting, but in refreshing your memory, who covered the costs of the displaced Croats? Was it the Defence Department or the Office for the Displaced Persons and Refugees?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Those expenditures, in relation to fuel, were charged to the Office for Refugees, who were receiving refugees. That particular amount of fuel was not charged to the Defence Department, but to the Office for Refugees.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So in budgetary terms, Mr. Stojic is right to intervene along those lines or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course. His budget was increased due to certain costs that were not down to his department.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Right. So this text concerns displaced Croats, but let's take an assumption, a hypothesis, that it would be Muslims, say, displaced. Who would -- who should pay the cost for displacing the -- the displacement cost of these Muslims, the Department of Defence or the office?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There were no requests to cover such expenses. I don't know who bank-rolled that or indeed in what way. In the HVO HZ-HB, no one addressed us requesting that the costs of transportation or travel be covered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott. Mr. Scott, I think you made a mistake, because the text applies to the displaced Croats, not the Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I didn't think so, Your Honour, but if I did, I stand corrected. My point was not -- my point was one of process, not of the particular issue. I did follow up with a question, Your Honour, that using that again as an example, what I tried to do several times is show the witness a particular document, a particular instance, address that point and also make the point more generally, and my follow-up question was when the Muslim men, which I put to the Chamber there's been abundant evidence of that, whatever the other circumstances, were arrested and held throughout the summer of 1993, my question to the witness was where the funds came from to do that. That was the question, and I don't think I was mischaracterising the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, the questions that were put to you by some of the accused in this case or, excuse me, their Defence attorneys, about the funding, and about the request for funds, and about the potential shortage of funds, let me ask you this: You and others have gone to considerable lengths to show how difficult it was for Herceg-Bosna to operate under these undoubtedly difficult times and circumstances. It's fair to say that the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina, the so-called Sarajevo government, faced similar challenges and difficulties, financial and otherwise; correct?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And I take it, sir, that to the extent that Croats were held and detained by the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina or their representatives in inhumane conditions and mistreated, I take it, sir, that you would not say that was okay because the BH government couldn't afford to do otherwise, or would you?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat the answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... your answer, sir.

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is not right at all that the conditions were what they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did you and other members of the HVO government and the Herceg-Bosna leadership know, during the -- during 1993 and around this period of time that we've been discussing, that there were various what some people would call extremists and hard-liners among you?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a lot of labelling going on in the media.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Would you consider that some of these people were known to be actively involved in the HVO?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand the question, these people being involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... the leadership of the HVO, the government of which you were a member, the government, the meetings which you attended on a weekly basis, the conversations that you had with your very good friend and close associate, Mr. Prlic, did you ever discuss amongst yourselves at the time, "Well, you know, it's true, there are certain extremist and hard-liners among us who are causing a number of problems," or are you telling the Chamber that was simply nothing you ever discussed in 1993 and 1994?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already testified that I had problems with some presidents of the municipal councils and that we settled this in this manner because they were persistently trying to implement their own decisions, their own regulations, so I felt that because of the way they were, they didn't want to accept or implement the regulations of the HZ-HB. And I spoke about those people, I wrote about them, and I communicated with them directly in order to make them implement the HZ-HB regulations.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let's go to Exhibit P07570 in the second binder, please. P07570. This is a record of a presidential meeting in Zagreb with President Tudjman on the 12th of January, 1994. The record will show that among other persons involved in this meeting were Mr. Jadranko Prlic. If I could ask you, please, to turn to page 62 of that record, page 62, the second half, the lower half of the page. President Tudjman: "All right, tell me, have they perpetrated crimes in Krizancevo Selo?" "That's right. Please do not delude yourselves again do you know whom they have removed. They have removed those who fought each other, you see." "And I want to tell you something else, and we should be aware of this. They are howling against Mercep to me, but, gentlemen, I too am against that. But this is a life-and-death struggle from Vukovar to Gospic, and if it hadn't been people like these men, we would not have Croatia. Let's get that clear. We need to understand that. I'm a man who came out of the war without having seen a weapon, but likewise, I know that that is what their objections are against the Croatian radicals. If it hadn't been for such men, we wouldn't have Croatia." And wasn't the same thought expressed, sir, and discussed among the HVO or Herceg-Bosna leadership; there were extremists, there were hard-liners, but they were necessary to get the job done? Isn't that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was not discussed at the sessions of the HVO. I already talked about what was discussed, about people who obstructed the HVO HZ-HB.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let's turn, please, to Exhibit P0 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness -- one moment, Mr. Kovacic. The Prosecutor drew your attention to a statement made by Mr. Tudjman on page 62. Tudjman was reacting following crimes committed in that location of Krizancevo Selo, which I'm not aware of. Tudjman seemed to sort of take some distance from the Croatian radicals, and he said so. As far as you know, where would you put President Tudjman? Would he be a radical, a hard-liner, a moderate, a liberal? Where would you -- how would you range him, how would you qualify him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can share with you my own position. I believe he was, above all, a general, a military person, in the way he reasoned. He knew what he wanted. He was running an overall project to establish a Croatian state, and this project eventually came to fruition.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You are telling us that he was a general but politically, it's hard to place him anywhere?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Politically, he has been described as the president and founder of a party that was essentially a peoples' party belonging to the conservative block. So that would be the background.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Kovacic. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I think again there is a misunderstanding here in the transcript, and that is why you needed to ask the additional question. As far as I know, all reservations aside, towards the end of 1993 it was Croats that came to grief in Krizancevo Selo during an offensive launched by the BH Army. I think it was featured in some indictment. I can't remember which one. If that is true, then the context of this conversation is entirely different altogether. We can't understand this if we don't understand the event we are discussing. The Prosecutor is asking a question based on this excerpt from the transcript without the proper context. This is unfair on the witness. He can't be expected to give us a personal assessment without knowing exactly what this is about.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if I may, I think the intervention by Mr. Kovacic is very significant. I would like to say that this is indeed a crime that was committed in Krizancevo Selo on the 22nd of December, 1993. We have the reports of the British officers there. A total of 74 Croatian civilians were killed. This murder was perpetrated by a Muslim faction within the BH Army. There is the discussion that precedes this quote by President Tudjman, and the discussion clearly shows that the crime was perpetrated by the Muslim Army. I think it's important to be familiar with the background here. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We've got the context now. Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, to respond to this, and not time for questioning the witness, but again given all the interventions, Your Honour, it's the Prosecution's use of this document that has now been mischaracterised, and it seems to be -- this seems to be a recurring pattern now. I put to the Chamber the Prosecution's view and the Prosecution's use of this document is that, in fact, it illustrates the very point I was trying to make half an hour ago. This was a topic about crimes, crimes being committed in this conflict on all sides. Mr. Tudjman starts on one topic, the first two -- the first three lines of that transcript under "President," and then he goes on to talk much more broadly. He changes his topic, and then he starts talking about Mercep, a Croat, then he starts talking about from Vukovar to Gospic, and all -- and we wouldn't have Croatia. He wasn't talking about Muslims when he says, "If it hadn't been for like these people -- people like these people, we would not have Croatia," Your Honour. So, I mean, can we -- if we could move away from this constant commentary argument about what documents mean or don't mean, we would be able to conclude this inquiry.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just briefly, please. My learned friend, and I don't doubt his knowledge, has now touched upon the fundamental problem. The words of Mr. Tudjman in these presidential transcripts are not just here, the reference that he has just mentioned, but in many other references, too, were not consistently recorded, the recordings were not complete. And in addition to that, we, who have been reading him for many years, know that President Tudjman would normally start off on one topic and then there were endless digressions, and then he would pick up the original thread some time later. If I may just complete this. It is for this reason that it is unusually difficult to use these transcripts. What I'm trying to say, the Prosecutor cannot possibly put this to a witness who doesn't have the transcript. He can't have these shoved under his nose to read, because the witness simply cannot understand. Even I don't understand them more often than not. This is simply not fair. There is no jurisdiction in the world where a witness can be examined like this. That's the point. Let them use another example, something far more transparent and clear. That is my drift. I don't think this is fair on the witness. If you don't think so, fine, your decision, but I'm perfectly entitled to say that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Well, I think it's very far-fetched. What is here, at least to me, and I'm sure I'm not the only one, is very clear, and all the comments were actually really not to the point. Please continue, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, my point to you, and this goes back to the point -- in spite all the interventions, this goes back to the point I started to ask you about 20 years ago, and that is -- and I'm using this simply, sir, to illustrate the point, and I put it to you this is a conversation, statements by President Tudjman in the presence of Jadranko Prlic, and I use it simply as a further launching pad, if you will, coming back to my question to you. And I put to you -- let me do it this way, then: I put to you, sir, that you, the HVO leadership, Mr. Prlic, Neven Tomic, those amongst you, you knew that there were extremists or hard-liners among you, among the HVO, who were carrying out atrocious acts, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Atrocities are something that we had heard of. As for individuals, the HVO never discussed that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You never discussed atrocities that were being reported in the press as carried out by the HVO, when Achmici happened and was reported around the world as an atrocity, when Stupni Do happened and was reported around the world and was a topic of discussion at the United Nations Security Council within days, within a few days of it happening, and it was reported in all the local and regional press, you -- my goodness. The HVO government never discussed that?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would like to draw your attention to one thing. The witness's answer was mis-recorded in lines 23 and 24 of the previous page. The witness did not say this. Lest I should testify myself and tell you what the witness said, perhaps we should ask the witness to repeat again what he said about the events, themselves, and what he said about individuals who allegedly committed crimes, and I don't think there was any mention of the HVO. And then I think Mr. Scott might think better in terms of phrasing his question. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said we never discussed individuals at any meetings of the HVO. We had heard about those events, we condemned those events, but we didn't discuss any particular individuals, because this was not something that we were meant to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, let's discuss some individuals. Let's go, please, to Exhibit P09078, and I'd like you to turn to page -- page 29, and you'll find it -- I believe you have excerpts. I believe what's in the binders will be excerpts, and if you have -- you're working in English, I'll ask you to turn to page 85. If you're working in Croatian, I think you'll find it on page 29. If you want it in e-court, I believe it will be page 122.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In this document, sir, which is a statement by Mr. Prlic which has been admitted into evidence in this case, this is a statement -- I want you to be very clear. This is a statement by Jadranko Prlic. On the page that I've just directed you to, Mr. Prlic says: "... in referring to the HVO, the war was fought by political leaders through the Main Staff of the HVO, actually through the military organs. As in any war, you could see the effects of the war through destruction, people who get killed, people who get captured or imprisoned, and also refugees. Military authorities fought war, and in that way they 'produced' prisoners of war, they were 'produced' in that way." Now, Mr. Prlic says the war was fought by political leaders. Who were the political leaders on the Bosnian Croat side who fought this war, according to what Mr. Prlic says?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The supreme commander of the Armed Forces of Herceg-Bosna was the president of the HZ-HB.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And who was that?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Boban.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And who else were the political leaders of the HVO, besides Mr. Boban, because the word used by Mr. Prlic is in the plural, it didn't say singular, " ... fought by political leaders through the main staff of the HVO." So we have Boban. Who else?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was the Presidency of the HZ-HB which Boban presided over.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You're saying the Presidency of HZ-HB carried out the war?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You asked me about the political leaders. Those were the political leaders at the time. The HVO was the executive.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: The HVO. And how about the HVO HZ-HB, were they among the political leaders who fought this war through the Main Staff of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The HVO is the executive. I don't see the HVO as --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I know they're the executive.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note, one speaker at a time, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: My apologies to the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, political leaders, I put it to you -- well, are you saying that the people -- people like Mr. Prlic, people like yourself, people like the other members of the government, you do not consider them to be political leaders; is that the distinction you want us to make?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I see. Who were the founders of Herceg-Bosna who were involved in such orders?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, a critical response of the witness was not recorded in the transcript, when it comes to overlapping between the Prosecutor and him. He explicitly said something, and in the meaning, "I know I did not consider myself a political entity," something to that extent. I will not -- the best thing would be for him to be asked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, there's something missing in the transcript?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I said that I did not consider myself, as a member of the executive, a political leader. We were an executive body.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, you referred to -- among these political leaders who fought the war, you referred to the Presidency of the HZ-HB. I take it, sir, that you'll recall that during about a 12-month, 15-month period, the Presidency only met twice, so I take it you would agree with me, sir, that the HZ-HB was not prosecuting this war on any sort of active leadership basis, were they?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would not agree with that. Members of the Presidency of the HZ-HB were presidents of the municipalities who, to a large extent, bank-rolled units in their own respective areas, and this went on like that until 1994. They, themselves, bank-rolled their units.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let's go on --

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Accordingly --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let's go on, please, to page 121 and 122 of the English version, pages 18 to 19 in the Croatia language, e-court page 162, 163. At that passage, in that passage, Mr. Prlic says: "It's a large --" when it's asked about who was responsible and who, according to him, was trying to shift responsibility for HVO crimes to him, Prlic: "It's a large list of people, of persons who are trying to shift their responsibility for what was committed, what has happened, on to the back of the HVO HZ-HB. Such persons included Pero Markovic, Jozo Maric --" excuse me one moment, please, a number of -- "Mijo Tokic," I'm not going to list them all, "Ante Jelavic, a whole circle of people from the army, I don't know, even know those names. It would really be a large list, a long list." Question: "How about Bruno Stojic?" Going down further on the page: "Is he one of the people who used you?" "Yes, if you mean in that respect." Line 12: "And how about Valentin Coric, where do you put him? Was he one of the people who used you?" "Yes, well, yes, he was against me, but I don't know whether this term he used me or this expression can be used with respect to him, because I used that term and I explained how I was 'used', but I don't know whether this can be used when talking about him." "Well, why was he against you?" Answer, Prlic: "You need to ask him, you would need to ask him, but it is quite clear from everything that he was against me. We were too different. We had two different concepts. We were on two different sides of the world." Now, do you agree and support Mr. Prlic's comments, that these were the people that he says were against him, Pero Markovic, Jozo Maric, Ante Jelavic, Bruno Stojic, Valentin Coric?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I've pointed out already, all those who were not implementing the regulations of the HVO HZ-HB were against us, us who were members of those bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If you --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If the gentleman would be allowed to finish his answers. This is the second time he's interrupted him in a row. If he could kindly be allowed to answer -- you know, give a full answer before -- you know, if he wants to pounce on it and be ugly about it, fine, but at least let him answer the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour, it's not being ugly, and again -- again, you know, Mr. Karnavas, as usual, has two sets of rules, the ones that apply to him and ones that apply to everybody else. When he was in the Prosecution case, he put things to the witness, he demanded a short answer, and he was constantly complaining about the lack of time. I have time constraints, too. I think the witness can give a direct question [sic]. My question was:

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Was Bruno Stojic one of those persons; "yes" or "no," sir?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that Mr. Prlic, while talking to me, complained about Mr. Stojic, that he was not receiving sufficient information, what was being done, and how it was being done, something along these lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. Prlic says, "Bruno Stojic was against me," not that, "I wasn't getting enough information"; correct?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If that's his assessment, if that's what he believed. I'm just telling you what I know about that. I know that there were problems. I know that there was insufficient information, lack of communication, and so on and so forth, and that this was the real cause of the rift between the two.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: How about Valentin Coric? When Mr. Prlic says, "We were on two different sides of the world," what was the relationship and the dealings between Mr. Coric and Mr. Prlic?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know about that. I did not really know Valentin Coric that well at the time. I can't judge this one.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Isn't it correct, sir, that on the political or government side, it was the people in the highest leadership positions who were responsible for what happened? A government prosecutes a war through the military, but it's the civilians who set policy; correct?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot agree that a government runs a war. I, as a member of government, never ran a war, nor was I involved. We were the executive. We were trying to help establish a system within the HZ-HB.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If you'll go, please, to page 128 in the English version, 128; in e-court 169; and in Croatian, page 25. When pressed for names about those responsible for ethnic cleansing, a topic that had been discussed at that point, Mr. Prlic says: "Yes. That could have been done only by the highest political leadership, president of the HDZ and vice-president, and this smaller -- the closed, smaller circle of the HDZ and the leading people who were members of the executive authorities in those municipalities where such things happened, such as Mostar, Capljina and Stolac. I'm quite sure that Pero Markovic was part of that circle, because his whole behaviour was in such a sway that obviously he hated Muslims." Now, sir, I put this to you specifically because this seems to be consistent with your theme that, well, most of these problems are being conducted in the HVO municipal structures. Do you agree that Pero Markovic was one of the people who was responsible for the crimes being committed against Muslims in Capljina and Stolac?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that Pero Markovic was president of the Municipal HVO and a member of the Presidency of the HZ-HB, a very influential person across the HVO units in Capljina. As for his responsibility --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: "I'm quite sure," Mr. Prlic says, "I'm quite sure Mr. Pero Markovic was part of that circle, because his whole behaviour was in such a way that obviously he hated Muslims." Do you agree with Mr. Prlic?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's Mr. Prlic's position. I would partly agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You would partly agree. Well, on what part would you agree?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We'll have to have a break.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I'll come back to that question after the break. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] After the break, do you have a question on page 129? If you don't have a question, I will have one.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sorry, I'm only hearing part of -- there's another conversation going on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was asking this, Mr. Scott: Will you have a question on page 129?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I don't believe so at this particular point, Your Honour, but I didn't get an answer --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Mr. Scott, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: My apologies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: But I haven't had an answer to my pending question, Your Honour, but I'm happy to come back to it after the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. With regard to the time you have used, I think you have 30 minutes left, at the most, but we'll check.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Registrar has the floor for an IC number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Just for the purpose of clarification, Your Honours, the IC number earlier indicated, which was IC 00888, is the number assigned to the list tendered by 3D. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Scott, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. Tomic, the question that was pending at the time of the break, and I'm sorry for the interruption in that respect, but I had asked you about the statements in connection with Mr. Pero Markovic, and you said -- we've lost it off the realtime screen now, but you said you agreed in part. My follow-up question to you was: In what part did you agree with the statement? And if it helps you, sir, among other things, what Mr. Prlic had said at pages 128 in English and page 169-170 in e-court, among other things, and again I don't want anything to think I'm misleading you: "I'm quite sure Pero Markovic was part of that circle, because his whole behaviour was in such a way that obviously he hated Muslims." And you said you agreed with Mr. Prlic's statement in part, so can you please tell us in what part you agreed with it?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I agree with the part of the statement, and I think that Mr. Pero Markovic is an example of a president of the Municipal HVO that opposed not only Prlic, so that was my remark, but other heads of departments had problems when it came to implementing the regulations in the municipality of Capljina, because practically they had to discuss everything with him, time and again, although everything had already been stipulated by the regulations of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Based on that, sir, I'm going to come back specifically to the context of Mr. Prlic's statement, and that is the person responsible for ethnic cleansing. So you agree with Mr. Prlic's statement that Pero Markovic was responsible for the ethnic cleansing of the Muslims in Stolac or, excuse me, in Capljina municipality; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was the president of the Municipal HVO, and I already said he had full control of the Capljina municipality. And as for his responsibilities, well, I am not the one to judge that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, I'm going to ask you one more time. You're avoiding my question, sir. My question to you, specifically, is: You agree with Mr. Prlic that Pero Markovic was responsible for the ethnic cleansing in that municipality; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot give you a yes-or-no answer. I have to say that this happened in the Capljina municipality, where he was the president of the Municipal HVO, and responsibility has to ascribe for that kind of conduct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Very well. And weren't the top HVO military authorities also responsible for the crimes that the HVO committed?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot speak about the responsibility before it is established. We know that crimes were committed, and I really don't know who was directly responsible for them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Would you please go to, in the same document that we've been looking at, in English, page 74, in e-court to page 108. If you want to look at the Croatian, it will be in the part that is, unit 3 out of 4. I think there is a designation on the Croatian version. There's tape 1, tape 2, tape 3 and tape 4, and this is on tape 3, page 15, if you want to look at that. But I think it's also available to you in B/C/S. At that point, Mr. Prlic says: "Now, who committed the crimes? It is quite clear that HVO military units, members of military units committed the crimes, and therefore military authorities were responsible." Do you agree with Mr. Prlic?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that according to the information that I had at the time, that HVO troops did take part, but I don't know anything about direct responsibility for them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Just so the record is very clear, when you said that you know that HVO troops did take part, take part in what, sir?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that members of the military units did take part in the events in the municipality of Capljina, the ones that you were talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, Mr. Prlic's statement is: "It is quite clear that HVO military units, members of military units, committed the crimes." Now, it wasn't taking part in the actions or events in the municipality of Capljina, sir. You agree with Mr. Prlic that HVO military units committed the crimes, and therefore military authorities were responsible?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said members of military units and their military structure is responsible, therefore.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, if you go on to -- please, to page 82 in the English version, page 118 in e-court, and in Croatian it is tape 3 of 4 at page 25. Mr. Prlic, starting at the bottom -- for those in English, starting at the bottom of page 82, Mr. Prlic: "The way or the manner in which they occurred, especially the manner and the way they finished, they stopped, how they were stopped, they show that there might have been an order or orders, there could have been. Who issued such orders or who would issue such an order, I have to confess that I did not -- do not know, but I believe that such orders could have been issued by those who created -- who created that area, the founders or some of the founders of HZ-HB who wanted that part of Herceg-Bosna." And if I can actually, sir, if you'll bear with me for a moment, go up above the part that I started, it was my error and I take responsibility for this, if you go further above the page, Mr. Prlic actually begins that section by saying: "So as I said, I said that the soldiers, members of military units, were the ones who committed the crimes, or actually actions which could be described as -- was crimes, and therefore military authorities should be responsible, should be answerable for that. And how did that happen? There are two ways of trying -- of explanations for that, two explanations. First one was that there was an order which was simply carried out, or they, crimes, were committed under the impression that they have to be committed in order to defend the territory which they considered was theirs. Now, whether there was or were orders, I do not know. However, the number, the simultaneous ..." And that's where -- and I apologise again for starting at the wrong place, that's where Mr. Prlic goes on to say: "Based on the way things were done, the way things were stopped, the conclusion could be reached that there had been orders." And then we go back, sir, to the founders: "I believe that such orders could have been issued by those who created that area, the founders or some of the founders of the HZ-HB." Now, who would some of those founders be, sir, based on your knowledge and experience, on the ground at the relevant time during this conflict?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The founders of the HZ-HB were the presidents of the Municipal HVOs, HDZ and HVO, the municipal authorities, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And when Mr. Prlic above that also refers to -- when he says: "The military authorities should be answerable for that," what military authorities do you believe should be answerable for the crimes committed by the HVO?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think this is defined in the regulations about the structure of the armed forces, that there is answerability that must be observed, as is envisaged in that document.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Just continuing on the topic of war crimes, sir, I mean, you do agree, don't you, just so we can understand where you -- where you come out on this, you do agree, don't you, that people like Kordic and Cerkez, who have been convicted by this Tribunal, that they were responsible for horrible crimes that were carried out in Central Bosnia; correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I object. What is the relevance to this?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'd like to know what this witness's -- and I think the Chamber should know what his attitude about these matters are. It goes to credibility, among other --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Credibility of what?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Does he think these crimes were okay? Does he think these men were war heroes, like some people do? My apologies, Judge Prandler.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Regarding the credibility, you contest that on the opinion that he might have regarding the perpetrators of crimes. Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, do you agree or not that people like Kordic and Cerkez committed horrendous crimes for which this Tribunal held them responsible?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If the Tribunal attributed this responsibility to them, if it found them to be responsible, then I accept the judgement of this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, do you disagree with it?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said I accepted the decisions or judgements of the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: It's a bit like accepting fate, "I accept the weather today. I can't do anything about it, but I accept it." Did you agree with it? When the judgement issued its -- excuse me.
