When the Tribunal issued its judgement finding Mr. Kordic, for example, responsible for the crimes committed at Ahmici, did you agree or was it your view that, well, that, "There goes that Tribunal again, they don't know what they're talking about"?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, he indicated that he accepted the judgement. Now, whether he agrees or doesn't agree, it's impossible for someone who hasn't sat through the trial, doesn't know the events. How can he possibly agree? He accepts. That's the best anyone can do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, Your Honour, we saw --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas, the witness, who was minister, is capable of answering any question, whatever the degree of difficulty. It's a personal question that is put to him. Then he can give a personal answer. Witness, Mr. Scott has put a question to you. You can -- can you answer, not answer? You're free to decide.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said that I accepted the decision or the judgement of this Tribunal in that case. I personally think that the judgements are too strong, I would say too harsh, in light of the responsibility of those people. But as to the crimes actually being committed, they were committed, they did happen, and I'm all in favour of the perpetrators being brought to justice.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, if you will turn to -- I believe this will be the last exhibit that I will show to you, which I'm sure will be good news to everyone. Exhibit P08489.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to stay on this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Tomic, it appears that on the 9th of May, 1993 - this is an important date - in the indictment it is indicated the 9th of May, 1993, the HVO attacked in Mostar the Muslim positions. The Defence challenges this view and seeks to establish, and may well do this through its witnesses, that it's the BiH that attacked on the 9th of May in Mostar. It so happens that on page 129 of Mr. Prlic's statement, in the presence of Mr. Scott, who was leading the hearing, but there's no need to look - I'll summarise the contents - it so happens that on the 9th of May, 1993, Mr. Prlic is in Makarska, probably on the beach, and on that day, which is an important date, he explains that he receives a telephone call on the events of the 9th of May, and he also indicates that you, you will have discussions with him about this matter because you, yourself, are also in Makarska. Now, do you recall these events of the 9th of May when Mr. Prlic is in Makarska, you are also there, and in the light of what Mr. Prlic says, he seems to discover what is happening? So what can you tell us about that event, where you are a key witness, because in fact your name is cited as being someone who called Mr. Prlic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. On the 9th of May, we were in Makarska, visiting families, because my family and Mr. Prlic's family, they were both in Makarska. And that morning, I received a call from Mr. Azer Sirko, who was a good friend of ours. We knew him well, and we have seen his name in the documents. He was the chairman of the executive board of the Elektroprivreda company in the HZ-HB at the time. He called me and he said his parents had been taken to the stadium and that a conflict had broken out in Mostar, that there was shooting and that people were being taken to the stadium. I talked to Mr. Prlic, I went to his place. In the meantime, he had contacted Mr. Zubak, I believe. He was in Citluk at the time, and we headed back to Mostar. In Citluk, we were --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me stop you there. In your view, is Mr. Prlic discovering the situation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. He learned about what was going on in Mostar from Mr. Sirko's call.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Both of you returned in the same car. That's what Mr. Prlic says. I assume that in the car, the road is a long one, you no doubt spoke to one another, because your return journey seems to be rather hurried. In your recollection, what did Mr. Prlic say to you about this succession of events, because now with the Azer Sirko call, you know that there were arrests, that events were happening? So what does Mr. Prlic say to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it was a very difficult voyage for us, because we were trying to use the mobile phone and the connectivity was very poor, the reception was poor. We tried to call various people, our friends, but it was very difficult, and we were quite astonished by this development. It was really a very troublesome situation, because in Mostar the situation had been tense, but we did not expect that it would escalate into open conflict. When we reached Citluk, we met with our drivers who had come to pick us up. We went into the town. We saw that there was fighting around Vranica. We saw the plumes of smoke, and the information that we received at that time from the people in Mostar was that in Bijelo Polje that morning there had been an attack, an act of treason, that was the explanation proffered by them, and that things escalated into conflict from that point onwards.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Final question. So you're in the vehicle with Mr. Prlic, and you or Mr. Prlic are trying to obtain information with the mobile phone. Mr. Boban, Mate, is the army commander. Mr. Prlic has a function in the HVO. In your recollection, did Mr. Prlic try and contact Mr. Boban so as to have, at the very least, explanations regarding the events concerning a military operation in Mostar? Did he try and call him or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think he was trying to reach him, too, and the president of the Municipal HVO in Mostar. I can't now really remember. I think that the first information we received came from the drivers, when we met with them in Citluk, and then afterwards, when we reached Mostar, we got some information there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Scott, do you want to move to another document, which is no doubt the last one?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, we were -- I just wanted to be able to put this back into the context of where we were in my last set of questions. We were talking about Mr. Kordic and his responsibilities in particular, and I'd like you to turn, please, to P08489, P08489 in the second binder. Sir, while you're turning to that, I'll say for the record this again is a record of a meeting in the offices of President Franjo Tudjman on the 24th of November, 1995. If I can direct your attention, please, to page 4, I'd like to start there. Mr. Prlic is speaking at this juncture, and in that paragraph, the second paragraph under his name, it says: "Today, in the light of this newly-arisen situation with the raising of indictments by the Tribunal in The Hague, the president of the Croatian Democratic Union also submitted his resignation, and in that regard it's necessary to prepare the corresponding formal decisions, organise the preparations of running the party's central board, which would settle this matter." Continuing on to the next page, President Tudjman: "Did you discuss that?" Prlic: "Yes, we did. One of the conclusions from today's meeting was that a infrastructure and financial sundries should be provided for the preparation of the defence of all those who are indicted, also including full financial settlement in terms of jobs and accommodation for the families of those indicted. I think in that regard we'll do everything we can to a satisfactory level where possible at this time." If I can then direct you, please, to page 10, where Mr. Kordic begins to speak. Page 10, Dario Kordic, about eight or nine lines down in his portion Mr. Kordic says: "We give our full support to the overall Croatian policy and to you, Mr. President, because it's clear, as Mr. Prlic said, that along with the realisation of general Croatian interests, which is beyond question, there are certain things on the ground that need to be explained and need to be done." Then going over to the top of page 11, and our time is limited, but in the second -- in the first paragraph beginning on that page, Mr. Kordic tenders his resignation, having just been indicted by the ICTY: "I tendered my resignation, and on Monday I'll send it in writing to the Central Board of the Croatian Democratic Union of Bosnia-Herzegovina so you, too, then, as the president of the Croatian Democratic Union ..." And it goes on. If I could next direct your attention, please, to page 25, where President Tudjman is talking. The bottom of page 25: "You see, when they were preparing such a solution, our friends put a demand to me about Mate Boban. And to make it clear for you, and this was coming equally from Bonn and the Vatican, they were making threats about these indictments and so." Continuing on to page 26, skipping a few lines, if I might be allowed: "But I didn't say it then either that Mate Boban should be thrown on to the garbage heap of history. I asked and I'm sorry that he didn't get more actively involved in other areas. As soon as I heard that they had announced the indictment, I issued a decision to bring General Blaskic to Croatia, which was interpreted by even some ambassadors and others as an unwise move, but in doing so I proved that we'll protect people. And I said that these men who defended Central Bosnia, the Lasva Valley -- these are men," excuse me, "so Dario doesn't have to stay in that post," Dario Kordic," but you can be sure that we'll try for the other two and all the others, I don't know the others, but it was with pleasure that I read Skopljak's interview. Is that his name? Yes. So, therefore, we'll try to do everything possible to make sure no arrest warrant is followed through ..." Now, you were aware, sir, during this time, and you were still in 1995 -- still a member of Herceg-Bosna authorities and still close, of course, to Mr. Prlic, you knew that it was the policy of President Tudjman and his government to protect at that time the people indicted by this Tribunal, correct, to remove Blaskic out of Bosnia, to hide him, to protect him, to make sure that arrest warrants would not be followed through? You knew that was the position of President Tudjman and his government; correct?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Is it correct, sir, that in connection with Mr. Kordic, you participated in a fundraiser to support Mr. Kordic during the time that he was indicted and on trial at this Tribunal; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I took part in an auction of paintings in Siroki Brijeg, and all the proceeds were earmarked for the Defence and to assist Mr. Kordic's family.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And that was in June 1999; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the exact date, but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you to Mr. Tomic and thank you to the Chamber, and that concludes my questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Scott, for doing your best to finish within the time limits. Mr. Karnavas, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. If I could get the assistance of the usher to give me the podium from the Prosecution, and I would be most grateful.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Tomic. I'm going to jump around a little bit to see if I can finish with my redirect so you won't have to come back here again. So, first, if you recall, last week the Prosecution wanted an additional hour and a half to talk about confederation, so perhaps it might be a good idea, rather than looking at newspaper articles and speculating what journalists have written about it, let's look at the actual agreement, the Washington Agreement, which I refer you to 4D 01234. That would be at the end of the binder, 4D 01234. And I'm rather surprised that nobody looked at this today when they went through this with you. Do you have it, sir?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, you indicated --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas, if I had conducted the cross-examination, of course I would have used the document. But since the proceedings are such that the Presiding Judge does not conduct the cross-examination, he lets people go their way.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I agree, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If we could look at -- you talked about a transitional period and a transitional arrangement. If I could focus your attention to Roman numeral VIII. That would be on page 10 of the English version, Your Honours. Do you have it, sir? It says: "Arrangement during the transitional period." Mr. Tomic, if you have it, you can say, "Yes," and I can --

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you. All right. Well, let me go over parts of it for the record, of course, and then you can answer the question. It says here: "The two parties agree to establish a high-level committee which will prepare a draft Constitution of the Federation and coordinate other matters related to the implementation of the Framework Agreement." And then it goes on to say that the committee will start its work in Vienna on March 4, 1994. I believe you indicated yesterday, you did mention something about the Vienna meeting. And then it goes on to say: "Until the Constitution of the Federation enters into force, the present administrative arrangements will continue in effect everywhere in the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, unless the committee decides otherwise by consensus and except in the Mostar city municipality, which the two sides agree will be governed by the EU administrator for up to two years." My question is: Was this the transitional provision that you were making reference to when you said earlier that the administrative arrangements would continue until a constitutional arrangement was agreed upon by both sides?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right, that is the portion that I refer to in my speech.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, if we go on, there was a big hoopla about confederation, and yet we didn't see this part. If we could go to attachment 2. This would be on page 13, page 13. Let's not look at what's written in some newspaper article. Let's look at the actual document.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. I was criticised by Mr. Karnavas for the few occasions, let me put it that way, at which I made some sort of comment, and Mr. Karnavas does it on a regular, continuous basis, and it's not proper. If he could just put questions to the witness, please, without argument or comment. And I'll be happy if the Chamber takes time to explain the reason I conducted my cross-examination the way I did. This document is in evidence. Everyone can read the document. I did not want to take the time to read the document. I was interested in the positions of Mr. Tudjman and his people and not what the document says, which is in evidence and which everyone, of course, can read when they have time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: That's one way of putting it. Another way of putting it is it was trying to mislead the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Of course Mr. Karnavas would always say that. That's always Mr. Karnavas' position, which is --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: We put the document to the gentleman --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I think the parties should stop arguing. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Attachment number II, Roman numeral II, page 13, let's look at the actual attachment to this agreement: "Outline of a preliminary agreement on the principles and foundations for the establishment of a confederation between the Republic of Croatia and the Federation." If we go through it, it says: "It is anticipated that a confederation will," will, "be established by the Republic of Croatia (hereinafter Croatia) and the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina (hereinafter the Federation)." Then it says that there will be a preliminary agreement and a final agreement. If we go to Roman numeral I, it says that: "The establishment of a confederation shall not change the international identity or legal personality of Croatia or of the Federation." Roman numeral II: "The confederation shall ...", and then it lists establish a common market for free movement of goods and services, and then if we look at number 2, it also lists all sorts of other cooperative policies such as transport, energy, environment and so on. Roman numeral III: "Croatia and the Federation shall," shall, "as soon as possible enact internal regulation and conclude agreement under the auspices of the confederation necessary to establish customs, monetary union, defence agreements," and so on. Now, when you were asked questions about the confederation, did you have this document in mind, sir, the actual agreement and what was agreed upon between the parties?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I referred to this as part of the Washington Agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And since this was an agreement, and as a result of the Washington Agreement the federation came into existence, at least on paper, were all sides to that agreement, the Croats, the Croats in Bosnia-Herzegovina and the Muslims in Bosnia-Herzegovina, were they all obliged to carry out that agreement?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, if I can direct your attention to 1D 01530, 1D 01530. This is dated 6 April 1994, and when you find it, let me know. All right. This is the Law on Ratification of the Preliminary Agreement on the Establishment of Confederation between the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the Republic of Croatia. Are you familiar with this law, sir?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, I know you explained this to us on direct, but can you please explain to us whether both parties within Bosnia-Herzegovina, that is, the Croats and the Muslims, whether both made an earnest effort to ensure the realisation of this confederation?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Croats believed that this was an issue that was on equal terms with all the other issues from the Washington Agreement, implementation-wise. However, the Bosnian side was not in the least interested in seeing this part of the agreement implemented.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And what part -- and what part of the agreement were they mostly interested in?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First and foremost, the implementation of the annex that had to do with free access to the port of Ploce.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. So all they were interested in is how they could have a deep-water port as opposed to having a relationship based on an agreement that was negotiated and agreed upon at the international level; is that what you're telling us?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. Maybe Mr. Karnavas shouldn't lead. This is not cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What I can say is this: At the time, Mr. Izetbegovic and Mr. Tudjman signed an agreement on one border crossing straddling the road to the port of Ploce. It wasn't in our interest to draw -- to establish a new customs administration for the whole of the federation. It was just about that one border crossing. So that was the agreement pursuant to which -- or, rather, as a result of which clashes erupted in the then government, which led to the media reports such as the ones published in 'Oslobodjenje'. And this is something that we have already commented on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. You said it wasn't in your interests. In what sense? I'm not quite sure I follow you, interest to draw and establish a new custom administration. Could you please explain that part of your answer?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In keeping with the Washington Agreement, and in keeping with the federation, we had to build new institutions for the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina, including a customs administration. My own ministry prepared a proposal for a law on the customs administration. However, at the time the interests of the Bosniak side was focusing on the agreement as it concerned the port of Ploce, and then there was a special agreement between Tudjman and Izetbegovic saying that a special law should be passed on the Doljani border crossing and that this one should be opened as a federal one. Therefore, it wasn't about us doing all the border crossings, according to that regulation, but just that one border crossing. If I view this from the perspective of someone who was the finance minister at the time, it seems to me a nebulous idea for two presidents to be discussing and specifically arranging the opening of a single border crossing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, yesterday you were asked a series of questions by the Prosecution, where Mr. Scott was suggesting that it was sometime in the fall of 1993 that the Croat side was moving towards negotiating some sort of an agreement for this federation. Do you recall those series of questions being posed to you by Mr. Scott?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And now I just want to focus your attention on 1D 0 --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas, I do apologise, and I'm not objecting to your question, but I don't want the record to be mischaracterised. The questions I put to the witness, and I do think -- my apologies to the Chamber, but I do think this is an important distinction. The political dialogue at the time among the International Community, a number of people were moving in the direction away from -- it's the Prosecution case, away from the Croat position of getting their separate Croat entity, not that it was the Croat politics that were moving in that direction. Mr. Karnavas can put his question, of course, but I don't want our position to be misstated. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: In light of that, in light of that explanation, then it becomes even more imperative that we look at this document, 1D 02854, because this is dated 29 December 1993. This is from the Security Council. So we're not talking fall, we're not talking late summer. We're talking December 1993. If we see from the very cover of the page, this is a letter that's signed by Boutros Boutros-Ghali, who at the time was with the UN, we all know, and we can see 23 December 1993, the co-chairmen of the steering committee had issued a report. Now, if we could look at this, sir, and turn to the second page, we look at the annex where it says "Annex report of the co-chairmen of the steering committee on the activities of the international conference on the former Yugoslavia," and we can see from the very -- paragraph number 1, it does make reference to a meeting at the Invincible on 23 September 1993. There we see that on that occasion, you had President Izetbegovic, Mr. Boban, Mr. Karadzic, met in the presence of the co-chairmen, Presidents Bulatovic, Milosevic and Tudjman, Deputy Foreign Minister Churkin and Ambassador Redman, and a constitutional agreement was reached providing for a union of republics of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Now, due to time limitations, we'll skip down. Paragraph number 2, it says that the two sides -- two of the sides signed, but the very last sentence, "The Bosnian Presidency reported that their expanded assembly did not sign the agreement." We go to paragraph 4, and it says that the co-chairmen decided to pursue a two-track approach, a two-track approach to build upon the Invincible package, and to explore whether, by tackling certain problems in the former Yugoslavia together, it might be possible to create more options for helping to find a settlement in Bosnia-Herzegovina. It then goes on to say: "One idea that was specifically considered was the possibility of a territorial exchange between Bosnia and Herzegovina and the Republic of Croatia that would enable agreement to be reached on an outlet to the sea for the Bosnian republic." All right. Now, if we go on to the next page, and we can see under "Deliberations," that's Roman numeral II, paragraph 6: "The discussions that took place had the following aim: To build upon the Invincible package; to provide the Muslim-majority republic with a minimum of 33.3 per cent of territory." I underscore this, because these are the internationals that are making these proposals, not Croats: " ... to ensure the Muslim-majority republic access to the sea." Paragraph 8, again we see 33 per cent and 17.5 per cent for a Croatian majority republic, and of course the rest would be for the Serbs. And then if we turn to page 4, Roman numeral III, "Outcome." Outcome, December 23, 1993, this is the outcome by the internationals: "The situation following the decision held at Geneva on 21 December at Brussels and 22 and 23 December may be summarised as follows: There is an agreement among all three sides that Bosnia-Herzegovina should be organised as a union of three republics." "There is agreement that the Muslim-majority republic should have 33.3 per cent of the territory and the Croats should have 17.5 per cent." Sir, at the time were you aware that this is what was being negotiated and promoted by the internationals that were engaged in trying to find a peaceful settlement for Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and I know that it was also said that access to the sea would be made available somewhere close to the border between Croatia and Montenegro. So this was part of the overall background of all the story that was going on in terms of the invisible package.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. I think that concludes that part of my redirect, so now let's -- let me take you back to the beginning of your cross-examination, and that was last week sometime or the week before. So I will start off with where Ms. Alaburic first asked you a question, and this could be found, incidentally, on page 33971 on the record. Basically, it had to do with control, and the question was through financing and logistics, the civilian controlled the army, and that's how it's established and exercised. So the civilian control over the army is controlled through financing and logistics. Now, let me make sure I understand you correctly. To your understanding at the time when you were asked this question, what did you think the word "control" meant, and to what extent did you, as the head of the Department of Finance, was able to control the army at the time?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This isn't control in the sense of controlling expenditure. The Defence Department, as far as that segment was concerned, and I mean expenditures, was coordinating with the president of the HZ-HB, who was the supreme commander. Therefore, we would only earmark funds for the benefit of the Defence Department. Then there were annual reports, and these funds were used for the purposes of logistics, mobilising the work of the Defence office, and so on and so forth. There was no monitoring of these funds, nor was there any inspection, so to speak, over the Defence Department. It wasn't before 1994 that plans were made for the first budget, and then funds were earmarked for salaries and also for other special purposes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: But the question wasn't so much about the Defence Department. It was the army. Through financing and logistics, the civilian control over the army is established and exercised? That was the question. And so my question to you is: In your capacity, your individual capacity as head of the Department of Finance, did you control in any way the army by way of financing it?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that there was no control by the Finance Department. Funds were forwarded for the purpose of defence to the Defence Department. How these funds were passed along is something that only they can tell, and they did this according to their own programme.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. That was my -- and my next question was: Okay, your department wasn't able to control the army, but what about the government, the HVO HZ-HB, this executive authority? Did they control, and by that I mean did they give orders to the Main Staff on how to use this money if they didn't -- what to do, did they give them orders, and if they didn't comply with the orders, they would simply cut off the financing or the logistics in order to control them?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if I may, the question presupposes that the Main Staff took any financial decisions and then orders could be given. We have so far seen no evidence at all in this courtroom to the effect that the Main Staff had an account, to begin with, or indeed that it took any decisions on how funds were to be allocated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The HVO HZ-HB, for as long as I was involved in its work, never adopted any decisions on the kind of expenditure that was going on within a department, and the same applied to how funds were allocated to the Defence Department.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Karnavas. I would like to go back a little bit, where the witness answered that the Finance Department had no control. It's page 64, line 22, about to disappear. "How these funds were passed along," the witness said, "is only something they can tell, and they did this according to their own programme." Now, Mr. Tomic, who do you refer to by saying "they"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I meant the departments. As I said, the first budget was made in relation to 1994. Up until that point in time, funds had been earmarked and forwarded based on requests that individual departments were making and the decisions on how to allocate, too, were individual. Most of the funds were assigned to the Defence Department for defence purposes and also to the Internal Affairs Department. Late in 1992, there was a report on the work of the HVO. Another report was attached by the Defence Department on how the funds were used, but there was no control system in place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you. So who was it that allocated the funds to the department?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As you saw in that report in relation to 1992, some of the funds were obtained by the Defence Department from the Finance Department, which was under 5 per cent of what they actually needed. Other funds arrived from the diaspora fund, and this was something that was channeled through Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: And it was channeled directly from Zagreb to the Defence Department?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: And that was, then, about 95 per cent of the money that the department had at its disposal. You said 5 came from your department, and was that the rest or was there a third or maybe a fourth or fifth source of money for the Defence Department?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, it's not correct the rest of the money came from Zagreb, because the Defence Department was enjoying some proceeds from selling some goods, and there were other proceeds that the department was obtaining. By and large, the lion's share of the money came from the diaspora fund.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, if I could pick up a little bit from where Judge Trechsel left off, because this whole issue about having a budget -- and I know you discussed it a little bit earlier, but when you say that a budget was established, could you please explain to us, what exactly do you mean? Is it a line item where you could tell exactly how much money is allocated to certain areas?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The budget, in its proper form, was done for the first time for 1994, where you had the revenues and the expenditures per department and office and other beneficiaries of the budget. That is what the budget means, that you have to have the revenue side and the expenditure side.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And going again back to what Judge Trechsel had asked you, you had indicated that the money would go directly to the Defence Department. Did your department in any way or did the HVO HZ-HB have any authority or control over how that particular budget or that money that was going directly to the Defence Department, how it would be spent; how much for weapons, how much for clothing, how much for food ? Was there any control over that?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already said that the HVO HZ-HB received yearly reports, annual reports, about the expenditure of the funds, and this became a part of the regular report of the HVO HZ-HB. But no decisions were taken as to the allocation of the funds within the Defence Department.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, today you did indicate at one point that the municipalities were bankrolling their own units, and that was to a question that was posed to you earlier. And could you please explain that a little bit more so we have a full understanding, because you seem to be giving the indication that perhaps at the municipal level, a different procedure is in place?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I already talked about that. This was one of the big problems that we faced. The Defence Department also had to deal with this problem, and the problem was that some of the municipalities, such as primarily Tomislavgrad, Livno, Capljina, for a long, long time, I think that for these three municipalities it was up until 1994, they paid their units and they procured clothing and things like that, so that when we're talking about Tomislavgrad and Livno, after some pressure was exerted on them to implement the regulations of the HVO HZ-HB because of the fact that the presidents were founders and members of the Presidency of the HZ-HB, they obstructed those efforts up until the year 1994, when the Minister Martinovic at that time started dealing with those problems, clearing up the situation. Up until that time, they merely exchanged orders with the budget of the HZ-HB. They merely told us in the period of six months we'd paid such-and-such amount to the army, and then we acknowledged that as the payments into the budget, and at the same time we considered these to be payroll expenses. So up until the beginning of 1994, Capljina, too, for the most part of 1993, paid out the salaries and other payroll expenses in this manner.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Let's move on to another question that was asked of you, and the question was: "Were issues of military strategy discussed at the HVO HZ-HB meetings?" And then the question continued: " ... or were such issues discussed in other meetings held somewhere else with other people?" And this was on 33975 page. So let's deal with the first part of this question. To your knowledge, could you please explain to us what, if any, military strategy meetings were held at the HVO HZ-HB level?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the HVO HZ-HB level, there were no meetings to discuss strategy, and I don't think that under the Law on the Armed Forces that was actually within the jurisdiction of the HVO HZ-HB. And I'm talking about the law of the HZ-HB.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, are you aware, because the question went on, were such issues, that is, military strategy issues, discussed in other meetings held somewhere else with other people? Do you know if such meetings were held, and if so, where, and who were the participants?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about those meetings, but I assume that that was at the level of the presidents of the HZ-HB.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Are you speaking of the municipal level?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: The president --

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The president of the HZ-HB, as the supreme commander of the armed forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Did Mr. Boban ever come to have a military strategy session at any of the meetings with any members at the HVO HZ-HB to discuss, you know, operational issues as opposed to what was happening in the terrain?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't really give you an answer to that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, let me put it to you this way: Were you ever present, you personally, were you ever present when military strategy sessions, operational sessions, were being held where Boban is chairing such a meeting with his close advisers?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not attend any meetings where strategy was discussed. I attended several meetings in Siroki Brijeg with the presidents of the municipalities and with the Main Staff, and the agenda was the situation in the area of the HZ-HB because there was a need for us to get information about the situation, in particular when it came to Central Bosnia, in order to be able to assess how to proceed with our activities aimed at establishing the judicial system, the financial system; in other words, plans on how to implement the regulations of the HVO HZ-HB.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, let's start now where the cross began by the Prosecution. And the first topic, if I could put it as such, dealt with the issue of the work programme. And as I understand your testimony, and this could be found in page 34119 to 20 of the transcript, that is, you had indicated that the first real programme was drawn up for 1994. Do you recall saying that?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, well, this is the first budget for 1994, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. But when we talk about a work programme, and you say that this was the first one drawn up, again, what is this work programme about?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's the work programme about how to ensure that revenues would come into the budget, how to organise the institution within the Finance Department, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: What about the other departments; did they have work programmes prior to the first real programme that was drawn up, as you indicated, for 1994?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that each department made its own work programme, and then this was all integrated into a single programme of the HVO HZ-HB.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And to what extent were you, as one of the department heads, were you responsible to the acts of another department?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In line with the jurisdiction of the departments, the Finance Department had to ensure that the expenses are not greater than those that had been planned. I'm talking about the 1994 budget, the first budget. And when regulations and decisions are made or passed, the Finance Department provided its opinion as to whether the decision or the regulation would engender additional expenses or whether there are funds in place to actually implement the decision in question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, you were accused of being the finance man, quote/unquote, of the HVO or HDZ, this is on page 34121 to 22, when you were a member -- when you indicated that you were an associate member of the Crisis Staff. So, in other words, you were not just an associate member, you were the finance man of the HVO and/or HDZ; is that true, sir? When you were initially asked to assist the Crisis Staff, as you had indicated, this is prior to the Special Purpose Council being established, if you recall that part of your testimony?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do, I do recall that. In April 1992, I received a decision signed by the president of the Crisis Staff that I am put in charge of the finances regarding the payment transactions office and cash transactions in general.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And there was another individual that was assisting you?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the two of us, Mr. Senad Kazazic and myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, but the question that -- what the Prosecution was suggesting, or accusing you of, if I can use that word, is being the finance man of the HVO or HDZ. In other words, you had another agenda or was working for someone else. Is that the case, sir?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Karnavas. You have for the second time now used the term "accused." Do you take that from the transcript or is it your proper interpretation?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, when you say -- when you call somebody -- he put the question to the gentleman.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: No, no, you used this word, and I'm taking your answer that it's your interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, it's an accusation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: It's your interpretation that it is, because it was not as such formulated, was it?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Okay, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. While we're paused, I'm on my feet to make the same point, Your Honour. I don't think that's fair. Just like the Defence, the Prosecution is entitled to put questions to the witness. I put my questions to the witness. A number of them, of course, were leading questions, as is appropriate on cross-examination. They were not accusations, and there was nothing about that he was taking -- had any different agenda. I was simply asking questions about his involvement in the Special Purposes Council and the Crisis Staff. I don't think there was anything particularly mysterious about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: All right. I also do not think that this is a very heavy point, Mr. Karnavas. I just wanted to clarify. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: It may not be a heavy point, but if we're talking about joint criminal enterprise, and that's what I'm getting at, and of course I dare say that throughout the course of the cross-examination, this gentleman has been accused of being a member of the joint criminal enterprise, and I think anybody who says otherwise, based on the questioning by the Prosecution, I think, is sadly mistaken.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: My view, Mr. Karnavas, is that those that are accused are those that are mentioned in the indictment. Others may be put in the vicinity, but it's a formal matter, as I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Very well. I'll move on, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, sticking with that point, when you were a member of the Crisis Staff, were you reporting to the HVO or the HDZ concerning your activities with the Crisis Staff when you were initially asked to help out, when you were working with your colleague there?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Our authority did not entail any communication or any earmarking of funds for anyone, including the HDZ. The Crisis Staff had its member. I mentioned the lady's name. She was the municipal secretary for finance. But the situation being what it is, in other words, there was a complete breakdown of the system, a shortage of cash, the Crisis Staff then took us in and gave us this specific job; to communicate with the SDK and to protect the cash in the Mostar municipality. We did not secure any funds for the Crisis Staff budget or for anyone else. We merely passed regulations, and I said that it was already too late, but all we did was pass regulations to regulate the use of cash and the conduct of the SDK in this context.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Last week or the week before, I think it was last week, you were asked some questions concerning how the HVO HZ-HB operated, and again yesterday there were some questions put to you as far as how Dr. Jadranko Prlic would represent himself. And if you may recall, there was a series of rather sarcastic questions put to you about how Dr. Jadranko Prlic would represent himself. Now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I think "present himself," not "represent himself." How he would present himself was the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Present or represent himself. Well, I don't want to debate with you, Judge Trechsel, at least not today.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: In any event, if we could just discuss the heads of the departments. You indicated at one point that they would make proposals, but they were autonomous. Is that correct? Do you recall saying that?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, did any one member, any one head of a department, have the authority to move another head of the department? Let me start at that, in the general. For instance, did you have the right to remove the head of the Department of interior?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. What about the president of the HVO HZ-HB? I mean, after all, he has this title, "president." Did he have the authority to remove you?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we were appointed by the Presidency of the HZ-HB.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And that brings me to my next point. Who would then have the authority to remove a member -- a head of a department? If you were appointed by the Presidency, who had the authority under that system?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Presidency of the HZ-HB.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, at some point you were asked about whether -- you know, why didn't -- this had to do with the municipalities and the fact that at times they did not comply with the decrees that were being -- or they were not enforcing the decrees being passed by the HVO HZ-HB. And you were asked, "Why not send the military, the HVO HZ-HB military, or the police to remove them in order to implement those decrees?" How realistic was that question?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I've already spoken about this strange relationship, those who were supposed to implement the regulations of the HZ-HB; the Municipal HVOs, in other words, together with the departments of the HVO HZ-HB, but now we're talking about the municipalities where the presidents of the municipal HVO were responsible for that. They were at the same time members of the Presidency of HZ-HB, and we were supposed to report to them on our work and they were supposed to evaluate our work. And that was a constant conflict, where -- that all the department heads faced in doing their jobs. For all intents and purposes, they had to renegotiate things with the presidents of the municipalities about how the regulations would be implemented, knowing that they had those powers because they were members of the Presidency of the HZ-HB. So there could be no coercion of any kind. It was out of the question, in particular in the municipalities that had sufficient funds and that were able to finance the units operating in their area. And I have spoken about that recently.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If I could press you a little bit. We know that Mate Boban was the president of the Presidency. We know the Presidency is made up of the presidents of the municipality. First, if you could tell us, how did they get their positions, how did they become presidents? Who appointed them or elect them? Was it the HVO HZ-HB or was it through some other means or manner?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they were elected in the municipalities. The former municipal -- what was it that they were called? The heads of the municipalities became the presidents of the municipal HVOs and --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, what about Boban himself, how did he become president of the Presidency? Did he appoint himself? Was he elected? And if so, by whom?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can recall, he was elected by the Presidency of the HZ-HB. In the course of the transformations, he became the president of the Presidency of the HZ-HB. I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, you were asked about -- well, you were told that -- or reminded, I should say, that the Presidency did not meet on a couple of times. I believe it was during the period of 1992 -- late 1992-1993. And I stand to be corrected if I'm a little bit off on the dates. Do you know whether Mr. Boban had sort of tete-a-tete meetings with the presidents of the municipalities; in other words, not meeting them as a collective body, but whether he met them individually or had contact with them telephonically?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I know about this is that the president of the Presidency of the HZ-HB held individual meetings or group meetings with the presidents of the municipal HVOs. In a way, he tried to avoid holding the sessions of the Presidency of the HZ-HB, because many issues would be raised at those sessions and there were no answers, because many of the municipalities were flat broke and they sought answers, various options. So in most cases, he would meet with them individually. And let me give you an example. In fact, I've already given you this example. The decision on the war tax imposed on our people working abroad was invalidated in those meetings because of the pressure of the municipalities of Tomislavgrad and Livno, and it was never actually implemented in the form in which the HVO HZ-HB actually passed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If I could just ask one last question before the break, or we could take the break; whichever. I'm at your hands.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It might be better to have a break now. We shall resume at 6.00 sharp.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay, Mr. Tomic, if we could pick up where we left off. With respect -- the one question I wanted to ask you is: How realistic would it have been - we're into the realm of not just de jure but now de facto - for the HVO HZ-HB to attempt to remove a president of a municipality by way of asking Boban, himself, who was elected by the members of the municipality as the president of the Presidency, how realistic would that have been, how plausible under the circumstances?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, this was not really feasible. It's what I called a strange relationship between the HVO and the Presidency of the HZ-HB and the presidents of the municipalities who were at the same time members of that Presidency.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And while we're still with the HVO HZ-HB, you, as the head of the Department of Finance, were you responsible for the activities of any other department? Could you be held responsible, for instance, for the activities of the Department of Interior, just to pick an example?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat the answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Would you please repeat the answer, please. The interpreters didn't hear you.

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Each president of department was responsible for the situation in his own area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, you were asked a series of questions concerning the issue of currency or currencies, and at one point it was put to you -- it was put to you that Croatia was deliberately attempting to sabotage the BiH economy. And that would be on page 34160, and again it pops up at 34162, where it was put to you that by using the Croatian dinar, that was a means of carving out a Croatian space. So let's deal with the first question. To your understanding, did Croatia at any point in time deliberately try to sabotage the BiH economy?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never witnessed any attempts like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Well, to put it into context in the manner -- this question was posed in light of the fact that a large amount of the Yugoslav dinar, and I'm paraphrasing here but I stand to be corrected, the Yugoslav dinar was being dumped, if I could use that word, in Bosnia and Herzegovina, so -- and I guess -- so as a result of that, you know, that was an attempt, I guess, to sabotage the BiH economy. Now, you did give an explanation, but could you please explain a little bit more about that? How could it possibly be that the Croatian government is somehow trying to sabotage the BiH economy by sending Yugoslav dinar over the border?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The arrival of rather large amounts of Yugoslav dinar occurred before the declaration of independence of Bosnia-Herzegovina. At the time, we could speak of, under quotation marks, of course, an approach to the Yugoslav economy, if I may put it that way. Nevertheless, this Yugoslav dinar was printed. It was out of control, and by that same token, the dinar itself undermined its own economy. Therefore, there were no more than a few companies around at the time that were happy to accept the Yugoslav dinar. For the most part, they were the exception. All the rest went straight to the black market. If we look at Herzegovina, at the time the black market, for the most part, was under the control of people from the Sandzak area, Montenegro, and this was an organised business. Therefore, if you look at that particular environment, most of the dinars that came out of that environment would end up in what we might, for the sake of simplicity, call the rest of Yugoslavia that was still around at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, on direct examination you did talk about the use of the Croatian dinar and at some point also the German mark, but it was put to you by the Prosecution that by using the Croatian dinar, this was a means -- a means to carve out a Croatian space. So my question would be: Under the circumstances, in light of what was happening there, and you were there, and being an economist as well, would it have been realistic or possible to force -- to force the people living in that area, in Herzegovina or Central Bosnia, to force them to use a particular currency which they could not use outside Bosnia-Herzegovina as hard currency?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've said this already, and if you look at the documents, that is clear enough. The municipalities were introducing the Croatian dinar, but first in parallel with the Yugoslav dinar. And when the Yugoslav dinar could no longer be used to buy anything, it was discarded. The HVO HZ-HB took a decision to regulate the payment transactions by means of Croatian dinars. If any other currency had been imposed which could not be used to buy anything else, well, it would simply not have been in circulation, it would have been worthless.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, in light of what's happening around the world today, one hears one particular word, and that is the word "confidence." Does confidence, when it comes to markets, when it comes to -- especially when it comes to a particular currency, does confidence play a role in any way? And if so, how?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said during my evidence, confidence is key. I'll try to explain this by saying the following: Introduction of a convertible mark. In Bosnia-Herzegovina, after Dayton, there had been attempts, after the Washington Agreement, to impose the BH [Realtime translation read in error "Croatian"] dinar. However, it wasn't listed among the currencies in banks outside Bosnia and Herzegovina. There were no exchange rates, and you could not use it to exchange it for any other convertible currency abroad, the only exception to this rule being Sarajevo's [Realtime transcript read in error "Croatian"] National Bank. Therefore, the BH [Realtime translation read in error "Croatian"] dinar never spread throughout the Federation following the signing of the Washington Agreement, particularly because there was a certain amount of misgivings about the amount of BH dinar that was printed and the way this money was managed. After Dayton, a governor was appointed of the BH Central Bank. The first thing that happened is the National Bank changed its name and was now renamed Central Bank. This was the first step toward re-establishing some sort of confidence. The next thing that happened, a new currency was introduced, the convertible mark. And if you look at its very name, it brings to mind the German mark, which was acceptable for all sorts of transactions. Again, a matter of confidence. Thirdly, the International Monetary Fund unequivocally backed this project, establishing that the Central Bank of Bosnia-Herzegovina would operate along the principles of a currency board. There would be no primary missions, there would be no toying around with the value of the currency. From that moment on, the convertible mark became an acceptable means of payment throughout Bosnia and Herzegovina. Confidence, therefore, is key to how a currency operates, plus obviously a currency's economic background.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. There are a couple of corrections for the record, Your Honours. One is on page 81, line 14. The gentleman indicated the Bosnian dinar, not the Croatian dinar. It just left the screen. And then there might be -- I'm sorry, on line 18. And then on line 22, I believe the gentleman said that "Sarajevo," "Sarajevo National Bank." But, anyway, I think that we can cure that at some point.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Would you mind speaking closer to the microphone. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas, on line -- page 81, line 23, should that also be the Bosnian dinar, rather than the Croatian?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And as I understand, and correct me if I'm wrong, as a result of Dayton, the governor of the Central Bank, at least for the first five years, was a foreigner, a New Zealander, as I recall; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. At first, it was a Frenchman, who was then followed by a governor from New Zealand, who outstayed his Dayton term of office because he enjoyed the backing of all the sides involved. Again, it was a matter of confidence because he was a neutral.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. The next topic I want to discuss rather briefly is the issue of customs. And it was put to you, and I'm going to be making reference to, essentially, for the record, questions that were put to you on pages 34192, 34201, 204, and there was another one on 34203, and it was put to you essentially that monies were collected from customs but never went to Sarajevo, to the Sarajevo government or the BiH government, and you confirmed that. And then it was put to you that this was a political decision not to send money to BiH government, and it wasn't because the money could not be sent to the BiH government. That was the essence of the questioning by the Prosecution. So let me begin by asking you, first of all, was Sarajevo at that time, the BiH government, were they making contributions to the funds, as they were supposed to be making?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course not. The Bosnia-Herzegovina budget had not been adopted for 1992, or indeed for 1993, I believe. It wasn't before late 1994 that the first budget was passed, a document based on which one could now manage the public finances sector.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: But the Prosecution put it to you that there were logistical offices in Zagreb and the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina was using bank accounts in Croatia and other countries, and therefore had there been a will to make contributions to Bosnia and Herzegovina, the money could easily have been deposited in those banks for Bosnia and Herzegovina. That was the essence of what was being put to you. And my question now is: Did the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina ever set up the necessary legislative instruments, and did they ever set up a bank account with various funds for contributions to be made, of course with the expectation that once the state would take its cut, the remainder would revert to Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. Before the witness answers that question, one of the things I was very careful to do during my cross-examination was to try to put some borders, if you will, on the witness's knowledge of these particular matters. During the course of his cross-examination, I think we established that Mr. Tomic at no time during this point in time between 1992 and 1994 was ever in Sarajevo, had no regular contacts there. I asked him specifically, "Who were your regular contacts in Sarajevo? Were you in Sarajevo during this time period?" And the information was -- his answers were he was not in Sarajevo, he had no regular contacts with anyone in Sarajevo. He also was never in Tuzla. He was once in Zenica, and he passed through in October 1992. So unless there can be some foundation for this witness knowing what the government in Sarajevo was doing, in terms of its bank accounts and legislation, I object.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may respond. It was put to him about Zagreb. We're not speaking about Sarajevo. We've already established that the banking system was not functioning because of the lack of communications. He already said that. It was then put to the gentleman by the Prosecution that: "Well, it wasn't that you can't -- you could not send the money to the BiH money, but it was a political decision not to give the money because there were banks set up in Zagreb by the BiH government?" The implication being, okay, deposit the money in Zagreb. And my question now is: Did BiH -- did the government of BiH set up the necessary legislation with the funds so they could be deposited, with the expectation that some of it would revert back -- or revert, I should say, to Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: That's partly right, and that's why in the first part of his question, you'll notice I didn't object. He has accurately stated that was the Prosecution position and is the Prosecution position, that had there been a will to make such payments by the Croats -- by the HVO to the BiH government, excuse me, there were certainly a number of means, I think -- we submit, we submit, that it could have been done. Now, that part was accurate and I didn't object to that. But now Mr. Karnavas has now changed to what was being legislatively done -- what was being legislatively done in Sarajevo at the time, and that's --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'll lay the foundation, Your Honour, because obviously this is an attempt to eat up my time, because we've heard testimony over and over again that a budget has certain funds and the money is channeled to those funds. It's not a matter of just depositing money in one huge bank account. Now, maybe that's how it's done wherever Mr. Scott comes from, but this was a highly-developed financial system.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: None of which has anything to do with the question put to this witness, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Not the one that I objected to.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Let me go back. Did we ever --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas, you can continue, because you have a technical expert in public finances. It is as if you were going to ask a question about penicillin of a doctor. Even if he is only a surgeon for knees, he can answer such a question. So I suppose that even if this witness does not know what's happening in Sarajevo, he's able, in some respects, to answer. So go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: The Prosecutor put to you that Zagreb had bank accounts, and bank accounts in other countries -- that the government in Sarajevo, the RBiH, that's what they are called now, did they ever contact you to tell you where monies could be deposited from customs to individualised funds?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Throughout the contacts that I had from the people who were in the Zagreb office, there were never any requests that were made about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: That's not my question. My question is: Did they ever notify you that they have a bank account in Zagreb with a number and the different funds, so then you can make your various contributions, and then thereafter, after they take their cut of the monies, the remainder would go back to Herceg-Bosna? Did Sarajevo government ever do that?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, you were asked about contributions to the state. Did the Sarajevo government ever make any contributions to the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna from the millions of dollars that it had collected and the monies it had laundered through the various charity organisations in financing its war?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'm going to object, Your Honour, not because -- I think Mr. Karnavas is entirely entitled, just so you'll know what I'm saying here, entirely entitled to ask him about whether funds flowed from the Sarajevo government to Herceg-Bosna in some fashion, but the second part of the question is pure argument and purely apparently for Mr. Karnavas' colour commentary, and it has nothing to do with the source, or the commentary, or whether it was laundering funds, but this is just --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Karnavas. Let me finish, please. Well, I'm making my objection, just like Mr. Karnavas sometimes makes his objections. It's not appropriate, Your Honour, just commentary by Mr. Karnavas again. But I didn't object to the first part, the proper part of the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: [Indiscernible] repeating yourself, and that gives really the impression that you want to take up time. It would be enough if you say things once.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If we could go, Your Honours -- if we could go, Your Honours, to several documents that are available. This knowledge is known to the Office of the Prosecution, because they hired a particular expert for the Delic case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me react to Mr. Scott's objection. I think that Mr. Karnavas has documents in support of what he's just asserted, so before you raise an objection, just wait to see how he's going to try and demonstrate what he's saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I know, but that's not the nature of my objection, and I apologise to Judge Trechsel if I didn't speak with 100 per cent efficiency. I think my record is quite clear on being one of the more succinct lawyers in the courtroom, and I'm happy to stand on the record of that if anyone wants to review the transcripts. The point is this, Your Honour: It's not a question -- the issue is not whether Mr. Karnavas has a document. I'm sure he has many documents. But there's no particular relevance in putting to this witness where the money came from. If he wants to make the point that the Sarajevo government was not supporting Croatia -- or, excuse me, the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, I didn't object to that part of the question. Now he wants to do something -- he wants to go into this laundering of non-profits, which has nothing to do with the question and is just to sensationalise the process. And he knows that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If we go on to document 1D 03126, I'm going to go through several documents and I'm going to ask you to bear with me and keep your answers succinct. Otherwise, I'll have to bring you back, and I'm perfectly happy to do so. 1D 03126. And we see this is a profile on the Third World Relief Agency. At the very top, it says: "By mid-1991, Bosnian President Izetbegovic contacts Hassanein, who he had known since 1970." It then goes down to say: "The TWRA," that's the Third World Relief Agency, "is controlled by a committee composed by Hassanein, and Hasan Cengic -" I believe you indicated you knew the gentleman or knew of him - "he is in charge of arming Bosnia militia run by the SDA party." Then if we go down, skip the names, it says: "All of them are important members of Izetbegovic's SDA party, and all but Ljevakovic were co-defendants with Izetbegovic in 1983 trial. Most payments require the approval of three of the five, except for amounts greater than $500.000, in which case Izetbegovic has to give the approval." Let me skip to another document, because the time does not permit us --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour, if I can try to assist. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm entitled to make my record with this witness, I'm entitled to redirect. And may I say one thing, that in the Delic case they hired a gentleman who specifically did a report for them regarding this. We're talking about $350 million, bank accounts, Silajdzic, Ganic, all of them were knee deep -- knee deep in collecting monies. And the question is, when he puts to the witness from customs what was going to the Bosnian government, it opens the door for me to bring this in. There lies the issue. If he doesn't like this, then he should not be doing cross-examination opening up a door, because the question is: Why was it that $350 million that came in from radical Islamic governments, where was that money going and why didn't they give the one-third or part of the cut to Herceg-Bosna to finance schools, to finance hospitals, to finance whatever needed to be financed at the time, or the defence? And maybe that's why the customs had to be kept.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have understood now. Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Your Honour, again, it's irrelevant. How is possibly the source of these funds relevant to the issue that Mr. Karnavas wants to raise, other than a general attack on Izetbegovic and the people around him, which is completely irrelevant to this case? It may have been relevant to the Delic case, I don't know, but that was a different case and there was a Muslim accused, and there may have been different reasons why it was relevant. I didn't -- let me be very clear, until the Chamber knows that I'm being measured about this. I didn't object, and Mr. Karnavas can make his point that he says the Sarajevo government didn't send its one-third to Herceg-Bosna. Now, I may or may not ultimately agree with that, but he's entitled to put the question. But where the money came from is completely irrelevant to this point. And the only reason Mr. Karnavas wants to get into this, because he seems to take some pleasure in saying bad things about Izetbegovic and the Muslims. He can make his point. It has nothing to do with where the money came from, did Herceg-Bosna get its one-third or not? It has nothing to do with where the money came from, and that's the nature of our objection. And I apologise if -- excuse me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll give my personal opinion. The argument of the Defence consists in saying that the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina was supported by countries sending funds, and we cite figures of $350 million, and that that money wasn't going to the Croat Republic. And we had elements of proof, as indicated by the witness, that as part of the budget, it included in the budget donations made by the Croatian diaspora, that meant that it was possible to balance the budget, and that de facto we had a financial system at the time where one of the belligerents receives colossal sums from funds coming from various states, and, on the other hand, another belligerent receives funds from the diaspora. There you have it. That's all that's the context of events. Very well, Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If we go on to 1D 03122, and it talks about, if we look at the last sentence going on to the second page, it says: "In the accounts and in the documents and in the bank accounts of the Third World Relief Agency, Austrian investigators have tracked $350 million they say flowed from Muslim governments and radical Islam movements to Bosnia." It goes on to the second paragraph: "The agency has operated several civilian projects in BiH since 1992." And then it goes to list them. Further down: "A Western banker in Austria referred to Al-Hassanein, as the 'bag man' of Bosnian President Alija Izetbegovic." Then if we go to another document, and this would be 1D 03115, I could spend several hours on this, but we won't, for time's sake, again there is a reference -- this is an article by John Pomfret, where he says the Western banker referred to Hassanein as the bag man. Then let's go to 1D 03114, and if I take you to page -- I believe it's page 7, going on to 8, this is under "Weapons instead of humanitarian aid," on page 8 at the very top, it says: "Intelligence data also indicates that over $2.5 billion US reached the TWRA from Islamic countries and that on July 10, 1992, then Bosnian foreign minister Haris Silajdzic signed a paper authorising Al Hassanein and the TWRA to collect donations for refugees in Bosnia-Herzegovina." And I won't go on, I'll stop at that point, except with one last document, 1D 03125, and this is in regards to Silajdzic, who's suspected of smuggling international arms.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: But let me ask you this question: Were you aware, was the Croatian community of Herceg-Bosna being told of the large amounts of money that the Sarajevo government was collecting, and was any of that ever offered to finance what the state government was supposed to finance at the regional or local level?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No amounts from these funds were ever channeled into HZ-HB. There was just a quantity of goods, the oil and heating oil that I was talking about that came in in the Ploce port, and it was used to keep the salvation route open.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If we go to 1D 03132, this is a text by an expert --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: 1D 03132, this is a text by a gentleman who actually was hired by the OTP as an expert. And if I could direct your attention to page 46, it says here: "Osama bin Laden himself is suspected to have donated large sums of money to the TWRA to finance the purchase of weapons and aid Muslim radicals within the Bosnian government."
